conservation.notes: Remains the most abundant turtle in North America despite habitat loss and road kill, because it can live in human-disturbed settings. Listed as S2 (imperiled) in Oregon, and as Threatened or Special Concern in parts of British Columbia.

human_tolerance.notes: Survives in polluted wetlands and artificially made ponds and lives in human-disturbed settings, which is why it is still the most abundant turtle in North America. It is crushed in quantity by lawnmowers and all-terrain vehicles, and nests on urban ground are taken by raccoons, dogs and cats.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Males start producing sperm in early spring, when they can bask to an internal temperature of 17 °C. The pair copulate in the water, and the female stores sperm in her oviducts for up to three further clutches.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Females only, between late May and mid-July. The nest is vase-shaped, dug in sandy soil often at a site with a southern exposure, and nests are usually within 200 m of water but can be as far as 600 m away, with older females nesting further inland. The female's optimal digging temperature is 29-30 °C. Two clutches a year is normal, though a female can lay five.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: During summer heat, or where vegetation clogs the shallows, the turtles vacate shallow marshes for more permanent water; these short overland migrations can involve hundreds of turtles together, and turtles moving between ponds carry seeds with them.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: In the north the inactive season may run from October to March. The turtle buries itself on the bottom of a body of water, near water in the shore bank or in a muskrat burrow, or in woods or pastures, and prefers shallow depths of no more than 2 m. Body temperature averages 6 °C while dormant, it does not breathe underwater, and it holds its breath until the ice melts. Warm spells bring it out even in the north.

vocalizations.description: Short, low-frequency calls. Turtles are popularly thought of as mute but make various sounds to communicate, and a study that recorded 53 species found that all of them vocalised; freshwater and sea turtles alike emit these calls from the egg right through to adulthood, and they may serve to hold a migrating group together. The painted turtle's own article records no call, so this is the group's documented turtle call, marked Low confidence for this species.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2443133 and family Emydidae from the GBIF Backbone record for the accepted name; iNaturalist taxon id 39771 from the iNaturalist taxa API; ITIS TSN 173783 from the ITISWebService scientific-name search, which returns Chrysemys picta (Schneider, 1783) as an exact match; Wikidata Q199203 from a Wikidata entity search for the scientific name.

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141, which points at the IUCN 'Least Concern' item; the article records the same conclusion in words, that its 'ability to live in human-disturbed settings has helped it remain the most abundant turtle in North America', alongside the Oregon S2 and British Columbia listings.

range.note: 'It lives in relatively slow-moving fresh waters, from southern Canada to northern Mexico, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific.' The three countries follow from that sentence directly.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'The painted turtle is a bottom-dwelling hunter. It quickly juts its head into and out of vegetation to stir potential victims out into the open water, where they are pursued', it swims out into open water and prefers shallow depths, and it walks overland between ponds and up onto a bank to nest. Those three sentences are the case for Swim and Walk.

traits.thermoregulation.note: 'Reliant on warmth from its surroundings, the painted turtle is active only during the day when it basks for hours on logs or rocks' and 'A cold-blooded reptile, the painted turtle regulates its temperature through its environment, notably by basking.'

traits.skin.note: 'Its skin is olive to black with red, orange, or yellow stripes on its extremities', over a shell of scutes, which the schema's Scales covers.

traits.respiration.note: Lungs, with the article's own note that while hibernating underwater 'the turtle does not breathe, although if surroundings allow, it may get some oxygen through its skin', and that it can breathe through the anus, or cloaca.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Females dig nests on land and lay eggs between late spring and mid-summer', and 'The nests are vase-shaped and are usually dug in sandy soil, often at sites with southern exposures', 5-11 cm deep. Ground, and the ground is not the water but the sunny bank above it.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the two adult averages the article gives, 'around 500 g (18 oz) on average, against the males' average adult weight of roughly 300 g (11 oz)'. The female is the larger animal and the one that makes the long trips up onto a bank to nest, so the middle of the two is used.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'The female weighs around 500 g (18 oz) on average, against the males' average adult weight of roughly 300 g (11 oz).'

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'The adult painted turtle is 13-25 cm (5.1-9.8 in) long'.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The longest-running study, in Michigan, has shown that painted turtles can live more than 55 years.' That is the best longevity evidence available for the species and it comes from a Great Lakes study, so it is used directly.

traits.diet.note: 'Although all subspecies of painted turtle eat both plants and animals (in the form of leaves, algae, fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects and carrion)', and for the midland subspecies of the Great Lakes, which is the one in northern Ohio, 'eats mostly aquatic insects and both vascular and non-vascular plants. In early summer, 60% of its diet comprises insects.' invertebrate 0.5 follows that 60% insect figure for the insects and crustaceans; graze 0.2 for the algae and aquatic vegetation; small_vertebrate 0.15 for the fish, since the schema has no `fish` tag; carrion 0.1 as named; and seed 0.05 for the vegetation it eats that carries seeds, which is also how the article says it disperses them.

traits.social.note: 'All ages bask for warmth, often alongside other species of turtle' and 'Short overland migrations may involve hundreds of turtles together', so animals are seen in groups at a basking log and in a mass movement, which is Group. The band is capped at 12 rather than the hundreds the migration figure allows, because one scene is a garden pond.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Reliant on warmth from its surroundings, the painted turtle is active only during the day when it basks for hours on logs or rocks', and 'The turtle starts its day at sunrise, emerging from the water to bask for several hours. Warmed for activity, it returns to the water to forage.'

traits.defense.note: 'Although they are frequently consumed as eggs or hatchlings by rodents, canines, and snakes, the adult turtles' hard shells protect them from most predators', and as adults their 'armored shells protect them from many potential predators'. A turtle does not flee or fight but withdraws into the shell, which is the schema's Hide; the armour itself is carried in the mesh rather than in this field.

traits.wariness.note: 'its ability to live in human-disturbed settings has helped it remain the most abundant turtle in North America'; it tolerates pollution, lives in artificial ponds, basks in company with other turtles, and has even been seen basking on top of loons that were covering eggs. 0.2 is a very unwary animal, which is what all of that amounts to, against the roadkill and lawnmower figures for the same species.

traits.senses.note: 'Their hearing thresholds are high in comparison to other reptiles, reaching up to 500 Hz in air, but underwater they are more attuned to lower frequencies.' Med is recorded because the schema's three levels have no term for a high threshold; nothing is asserted about vision, smell or touch, which neither this record's sources nor the Turtle article characterise for this species.

habitat.use.note: 'It lives in relatively slow-moving fresh waters' and prefers 'large wetlands with long periods of inundation and emergent vegetation', 'shallow[s] that contain dense vegetation'; it is 'very aquatic, leaving the immediate vicinity of its water body only when forced by drought' in the eastern subspecies, but makes overland trips to nest and to escape heat. The aquatic/ground split is authored from those statements.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: The cited winter shelters are 'on the bottom of a body of water, near water in the shore-bank or the burrow of a muskrat, or in woods or pastures', and it hibernates 'by burying itself'. That is burrow, and it is the refuge the record depends on; the basking log is carried as a perch instead, since a turtle on a log in the sun is using it as a platform, not as cover.

habitat.resources.note: The diet list for the feeding tags, with months from the article's own seasonal account: foraging starts when the water reaches 15-18 °C in spring and stops when temperatures fall below that in autumn, with 60% of the midland diet insects in early summer; `water` covers the shallows it hunts in and the pond it overwinters under; `burrow` the winter refuge; `perch` the log or rock it basks on. The seed tag carries the article's finding that 'As turtles move between ponds and habitats, they carry seeds along with them to new locations' and that it is 'effective seed dispersers'.

habitat.requires.note: 'To thrive, painted turtles need fresh waters with soft bottoms, basking sites, and aquatic vegetation.' The 200 m radius is the article's own figure, not an authored one: 'Nests are often within 200 m (220 yd) of water', which is how far the female will travel from the pond to lay.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'its ability to live in human-disturbed settings has helped it remain the most abundant turtle in North America' and 'its ability to survive in polluted wetlands and artificially made ponds has allowed it to maintain its range'. road_mortality is High from the two named causes, 'habitat loss and road killings', plus 'crushing by agricultural machines or golf course lawnmowers or all-terrain vehicles'. The numeric tolerances are authored around that.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'During winter, the turtle brumates, usually in the mud at the bottom of water bodies', and 'In the north, the inactive season may be as long as from October to March' while 'the southernmost populations may not hibernate at all'. Brumation is the article's own word, and the Lake Erie shore is squarely in the north.

seasonal.triggers.note: 'In the spring, when the water reaches 15-18 °C (59-64 °F), the turtle begins actively foraging. In fall, the turtle stops foraging when temperatures drop below the spring set-point.' Enter below 15 °C, exit above 18 °C, both over a week. These are the article's own numbers.

seasonal.phases.note: The spring sperm production at a 17 °C basking temperature, the female-only nesting window from late May to mid-July with its nest depth, distance from water and digging temperature, the summer overland movement out of clogging shallows, and the October-to-March inactive season with its shelter and body temperature all come from the article; the month boundaries are judgements aligned to those statements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg is a real stage here because the female lays a clutch of about 4.9 to 11.9 eggs depending on subspecies, the midland averaging 7.6. For the juvenile, 'Hatchlings north of a line from Nebraska to northern Illinois to New Jersey typically arrange themselves symmetrically in the nest and overwinter to emerge the following spring' and 'About a week to a week and a half after emerging from their eggs ... hatchlings begin feeding'; duration_days is therefore omitted rather than invented. scale 0.2 is a judgement: the article gives no hatchling length, only that 'The hatchling has a proportionally larger head, eyes, and tail, and a more circular shell than the adult', and 'Hatched turtles grow until sexual maturity: 2-9 years for males, 6-16 for females.'

vocalizations.call.note: 'While popularly thought of as mute, turtles make various sounds to communicate. One study which recorded 53 species found that all of them vocalized. Various species of both freshwater and sea turtles emit short, low-frequency calls from the time they are in the egg to when they are adults. These vocalizations may serve to create group cohesion when migrating.' The painted turtle's own article describes no call, so this is the documented turtle-level statement, marked Low confidence for this species; the schema's context vocabulary has no term for a turtle call, and Chirp is the closest. No recording is cited.

look.note: 'The turtle's top shell is dark and smooth, without a ridge. Its skin is olive to black with red, orange, or yellow stripes on its extremities.' The dark smooth top shell is the body colour, the pale olive-and-yellow underside and limbs the belly, and the red-orange marginal scutes that give the animal its name - the article's own 'red, orange, or yellow stripes' - are drawn as a narrow band low on the shell's edge rather than a shell-shaped overlay, because the article is explicit that the top shell is 'dark and smooth' and a full overlay hid the dark shell behind the orange in the previewer. No ridge or keel part is drawn, because the article says the top shell is 'without a ridge'. The proportions are authored for a broad, flat animal The proportions are authored for a broad flat animal from the 13-25 cm length, with a short neck, a small head and a very short tail, which is the shape the article describes and the mesh's quadruped plan can carry.

behavior.note: fsm-ground-forager-v1 is the shared program for an animal that forages when hungry, wanders, drinks, flees and rests in shelter, and the painted turtle's day is exactly that once the basking hours are done: 'Warmed for activity, it returns to the water to forage.' rest_sun_lo_deg -90 and rest_sun_hi_deg -6 are the program's documented diurnal settings, which suit an animal 'active only during the day'. food_tag is invertebrate because the midland subspecies of the Great Lakes eats mostly aquatic insects. Both gaits are walk, since a turtle never runs, and flee_m is cut to 8 m because its answer to a threat is to withdraw, not to travel.
